newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mugler stabs at couture with insects and S&M.
newsitem.headline: Mugler stabs at couture with insects and S&M.

text.p: French designer Thierry Mugler topped off the haute couture season on Wednesday, creating a high-tech world of insect women and whip-yielding Amazons for his first stab at the art of custom-made tailoring.
Mugler's trademark ultra-curvy hourglass suits over seamed stockings and stiletto heels turned nasty over leather panties, in creaky vinyl on a punk model, or with nothing but fishnet stockings.

Take an S&M version of the evening gown in latex, the sequin butterfly tapestry of a slinky sheath painted on Jerry Hall or spider web catsuits and you have an eery costume parade that is just a sideshow for the laser-sharp cut of a Mugler jacket or the graceful drape of a black chiffon evening gown.

"It was absolutely spectacular," said Dawn Mello, president of U.S. department stores Bergdorf Goodman. "It shows that he really knows what fit, shape and detail are about and how to make really beautiful clothes. If you strip away all that extra stuff there are a lot of terrific suits and evening clothes."
"I loved all the suiting which is his forte, it's what he does best," said Nicole Fischelis of Saks Fifth Avenue. "And I loved the way he did some of the chiffon dresses."
Earlier, Paco Rabanne's trademark chain dresses took on new colour, adorned with pink suction cups or an apron of coins.
To the violent beat of techno music, the models paraded coats that seemed crafted from multicoloured paper, metal bras hung with curtains and a hat peaked by a revolving disco ball.

His porcupine dress of protruding steel rods strung with dangling safety pins was pure whimsy while multi-coloured bands and floral motifs of metallic jersey ensembles can be translated into prints for a more realistic ready-to-wear line.

"For me, haute couture has become a show, it's not luxury ready-to-wear," Rabanne told reporters backstage. "It's really a game where we try to push technique and materials as far as they will go. After these experiments we try to adapt our results to the ready-to-wear. It's a kind of laboratory."

At Balmain there was no danger of making a fashion statement with U.S. designer Oscar de la Renta's ladylike bouclette suits in lilac, cyclamen or lime, just right for local charity luncheons and tasteful ivory jackets with Nehru collars perfect for poolside cocktails.

Wealthy Americans afraid to go off the beaten track will snatch up that curvy little black suit with pearl buttons, the garlands of Wedgewood flowers swirling around a sky blue coat with a matching dress or his bands of chantilly spiralling down a chiffon column.
And why not a white organdy empire dress embroidered with pearls for their debutante daughters' coming-out ball?

The skilled workmanship of Balmain's decades-old atelier showed through in a beautiful powdery yellow gown embroidered with lace and Beauvais point birds and a snowy tulle dancing dress, the bodice's black pearls speckling down the skirt.

De la Renta, who designed U.S. First Lady Hilary Clinton's inaugural gown, had a weighty front row line-up, including former U.S. secretary of state Henry Kissinger and New York socialite Nan Kempner.
